description: Platform-curated domain knowledge for the electronics vertical. Each statement is a self-contained, vendor-neutral sentence with explicit numbers+units so the narration claim guard can verify numeric claims against this text. No brand recommendations, no dollar prices.

entries.statement: Sustained local training or full fine-tuning of LLMs generally needs 16GB+ of GPU VRAM; 8GB cards suit small quantized models and LoRA-style fine-tuning of 7B-class models.
Local inference of a 7B-parameter LLM quantized to 4-bit typically fits in 6-8GB of GPU VRAM.
Local inference of a 13B-parameter LLM generally needs 10-16GB of GPU VRAM depending on quantization level.
Running a 70B-parameter LLM locally requires roughly 40GB+ of GPU VRAM even at 4-bit quantization, which puts it in multi-GPU or cloud territory rather than on a single laptop.
Full fine-tuning of an LLM typically needs 2-4x the GPU VRAM of inference on the same model, because gradients and optimizer states must fit in memory alongside the weights.
LoRA and QLoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning can adapt a 7B-class model on a single 8-12GB GPU, versus 16GB+ for full fine-tuning of the same model.
Knowledge distillation runs a larger teacher model alongside a smaller student, so the GPU budget must hold both at once - a 13B teacher plus a 7B student wants roughly 24GB of combined VRAM.
Long context windows inflate LLM memory use - the KV cache can add several GB of VRAM at 32k-token contexts on 7B-13B models - so budget VRAM headroom beyond the base model footprint.
Workstation-class desktop GPUs commonly carry 24-48GB of VRAM, a full tier above the 8-16GB typical of laptop GPUs.
Datacenter-class accelerator cards commonly carry 40-80GB of VRAM and are reached through cloud instances or servers rather than anything in a laptop chassis.
When a workload exceeds 16GB of laptop VRAM, the standard step-up path is a desktop workstation GPU or a cloud GPU instance rather than a bigger laptop.
Laptop GPUs top out around 16GB of VRAM in current generations, so workloads needing more must move to desktop or cloud hardware.
When a model exceeds GPU VRAM, layers can offload to system RAM at a large speed penalty, so 32-64GB of system RAM is a useful safety net for local AI work.
Competitive esports titles at 1080p run well past 144 FPS on an entry-level discrete GPU, and pair naturally with a 144Hz or faster display.
AAA gaming at 1440p and high settings is comfortable on a mid-range discrete GPU with 8GB of VRAM.
4K gaming or heavy ray tracing generally calls for a high-end GPU with 12-16GB of VRAM.
Modern AAA titles increasingly expect 8GB of GPU VRAM at 1080p-1440p, and 6GB cards may need reduced texture settings to stay smooth.
16GB of system RAM is the practical baseline for modern gaming, and 32GB helps when streaming or running heavy background apps alongside a game.
High-refresh 1080p gaming is often CPU-bound, so a recent 6-8 core processor matters as much as the GPU for sustaining 144+ FPS.
Smooth 4K video editing wants 32GB of system RAM as a floor, with 64GB preferred for multi-layer timelines and motion graphics.
GPU-accelerated 4K video editing and export benefit from a discrete GPU with at least 8GB of VRAM.
Photo editing on large RAW files is comfortable with 16GB of RAM and a color-accurate display, while heavy panorama or focus-stacking work prefers 32GB.
3D modeling and animation workloads want a discrete GPU with 8-12GB of VRAM and at least 32GB of system RAM for complex scenes.
Professional CAD work with large assemblies runs best on a discrete GPU with 6-8GB of VRAM paired with 32GB of system RAM.
Finite-element and CFD simulation is primarily CPU- and RAM-bound, where 32-64GB of RAM matters more than GPU class.
Gaming chassis with high-wattage discrete GPUs typically deliver 3-6 hours of light-use battery life, versus 8-15 hours for thin-and-light integrated-graphics laptops.
Performance gaming laptops usually weigh 2.2-3.5kg plus a large power brick, while ultraportables sit near 1-1.5kg.
Thin chassis throttle sustained GPU workloads, so the same GPU part can run 15-30% slower in an ultraportable than in a thick gaming chassis with robust cooling.
A high-refresh monitor only pays off when the GPU can sustain matching frame rates - a 240Hz panel needs the GPU to hold near 240 FPS in your titles to show its benefit.
Driving a 4K monitor for gaming demands roughly twice the GPU power of 1440p at the same settings, while desktop and video playback at 4K 60Hz is easy for any modern GPU.
For competitive play, a 1080p or 1440p monitor at 144-240Hz is a better pairing with a mid-range GPU than a 4K panel at 60Hz.
16GB of RAM is the recommended baseline for general, student, and office use, while 8GB constrains browser-heavy multitasking.
32GB of RAM is the comfortable tier for heavy multitasking, data work, virtual machines, and container-based development.
NVMe SSDs read several times faster than SATA SSDs - roughly 3,500-7,000MB/s versus about 550MB/s - which shortens boot, game-load, and project-open times.
A 1TB SSD is the practical floor for a game library, since modern AAA installs commonly run 100-150GB each.
AI datasets and model checkpoints consume storage quickly - a 7B-parameter checkpoint alone is roughly 14GB at 16-bit precision - so 1TB+ of NVMe storage is advisable for local AI work.

GPU VRAM tiers for AI work: an 8GB GPU handles inference and small/quantized fine-tuning, a 12GB GPU adds headroom for mid-size fine-tuning, 16GB is the practical floor for sustained training, and 24GB or more (desktop workstation class) is needed for larger models.

When a laptop tops out for AI training, the standard step-up is a desktop workstation GPU with 24GB of VRAM or a cloud GPU instance, rather than a higher-priced laptop, since laptop GPUs cap around 16GB.
